articles.title: I Built CouponLab with AI Help. The Coupon Codes Still Have to Survive Checkout.
articles.excerpt: There’s a very specific kind of optimism involved in copying a coupon code. You see “20% off.” You picture the cheaper total. You paste the code. “Coupon cannot be applied to this order.” Apparently,…
articles.body: There’s a very specific kind of optimism involved in copying a coupon code. You see “20% off.” You picture the cheaper total. You paste the code. “Coupon cannot be applied to this order.” Apparently, the optimism was the free part. That gap between finding a discount and actually being able to use it is why I’m building CouponLab . The approach is straightforward: I use AI to help discover offers, then try the coupon codes myself. CouponLab is also on Product Hunt https://www.producthunt.com/products/couponlab , so I wanted to share what I’m working on, where AI fits, and the part I’m still trying to get right. Spoiler: it involves more fine print than I would have chosen for myself. The problem sounded simple People looking for coupons want to save money on something they’re buying.
articles.author: Auu Cooper

articles.title: How to secure a Spring Security client application with OIDC (using pac4j)
articles.excerpt: If you already have Spring Security in your application, with hasRole rules, @PreAuthorize on services and code reading SecurityContextHolder and you want to add an OpenID Connect login, while keeping…
articles.body: If you already have Spring Security in your application, with hasRole rules, @PreAuthorize on services and code reading SecurityContextHolder and you want to add an OpenID Connect login, while keeping that authorization code, you can use pac4j for that. Whatever the provider (Keycloak, Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, a CAS server, etc.), once pac4j has authenticated the user, it can make that user available to Spring Security. The spring-security-pac4j bridge does this. It transfers the pac4j profile into the Spring Security context; it does not perform authentication itself. Adding the bridge alone will not give you an OIDC login.

articles.title: I Asked AI a Question. Then It Told Me to Put My Phone Away.
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass Most AI tools are designed to keep you talking to them. I wanted to build one that sends you away. OpenField tur…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built Most AI tools are designed to keep you talking to them. I wanted to build one that sends you away. OpenField turns a question about your surroundings into a short field study. You type something you are curious about, like "Which side of my street stays shady the longest?" , then add a place and a time budget (15, 30, 45 or 60 minutes). Local Gemma turns that into a small plan: 4–6 steps, the evidence to collect at each step, rough timing, and safety notes. Then the app gets out of your way. You can open a minimal Field Mode with a timer and big step cards, or print a Field Card and leave your phone at home.

articles.title: Why Java is Still the Quiet Engine of the Web (And Why It’s Not Going Anywhere)
articles.excerpt: There’s a long-running running joke in developer circles that Java is the "dinosaur" of modern programming languages. It’s heavy, it’s verbose, and everyone seems to move on to whatever lightweight Ja…
articles.body: There’s a long-running running joke in developer circles that Java is the "dinosaur" of modern programming languages. It’s heavy, it’s verbose, and everyone seems to move on to whatever lightweight JavaScript framework or shiny new language trend came out last Tuesday. Yet, if you look under the hood of almost every major financial institution, e-commerce giant, or cloud backend, there’s a massive Java application quietly running millions of transactions a second. So, why does Java stick around? Verbosity as a Feature, Not a Bug When you’re learning Java, writing System.out.println() feels like typing out a novel just to display a single word. But when you’re maintaining a legacy codebase with 500,000 lines of code across 30 team members, that exact explicit nature is what saves you.
